p.src: The opening question is a genuine paradox about composite particles. If two fermions make a boson, can two such bosons occupy the same state without violating fermionic exclusion? The answer begins with the exchange rule itself.

p.src:
Suppose two identical particles are described by a wavefunction of two arguments. The symbols $x$ and $y$ label the two particle slots; they do not distinguish two species. For bosons the wavefunction is symmetric, while for fermions it is antisymmetric: $\Psi_B(x,y)=\Psi_B(y,x),
\qquad
\Psi_F(x,y)=-\Psi_F(y,x).$ The symmetry says that interchanging the two indistinguishable particles does not produce a new physical state.

p.src: Two bosons can certainly occupy the same one-particle state. If that state has wavefunction $\varphi$, the two-particle product is $\Psi(x,y)=\varphi(x)\varphi(y).$ Wavefunctions are ordinary complex-valued functions, not operators or matrices, so their values commute: $\varphi(x)\varphi(y)=\varphi(y)\varphi(x).$ The product is therefore symmetric. The same construction cannot give a nonzero two-fermion state, because antisymmetry would require $\varphi(x)\varphi(y)=-\varphi(y)\varphi(x),$ while the two sides without the minus sign are equal.

p.src:
More generally, begin with any two-particle wavefunction $F(x,y)$, with no assumed exchange symmetry. Its symmetric and antisymmetric parts are, apart from normalization, $\begin{aligned}
F_{\mathrm{sym}}(x,y)&=F(x,y)+F(y,x),\\
F_{\mathrm{asym}}(x,y)&=F(x,y)-F(y,x).\end{aligned}$ The exchange check is explicit: $\begin{aligned}
F_{\mathrm{sym}}(y,x)
&=F(y,x)+F(x,y)
=F_{\mathrm{sym}}(x,y),\\
F_{\mathrm{asym}}(y,x)
&=F(y,x)-F(x,y)
=-F_{\mathrm{asym}}(x,y).\end{aligned}$ Adding the exchanged function symmetrizes it; subtracting the exchanged function antisymmetrizes it.

p.src:
A pair of hydrogen atoms provides the more interesting case. There are four constituent fermions: two identical electrons and two identical protons. Let $x_1,x_2$ denote the electron variables and $y_1,y_2$ the proton variables. The four-body wavefunction must be antisymmetric separately under exchange of the electrons and under exchange of the protons: $\begin{aligned}
\Psi(x_2,x_1;y_1,y_2)
&=-\Psi(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2),\\
\Psi(x_1,x_2;y_2,y_1)
&=-\Psi(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2).\end{aligned}$

p.src: To motivate two distinct one-atom wavefunctions, imagine one hydrogen atom localized near the origin, with wavefunction $\psi(x,y)$, and another localized elsewhere, with wavefunction $\phi(x,y)$. The second may simply be a translated copy of the first, obtained by translating both its electron and proton arguments, but it is still a distinct wavefunction in this setup. A naive product is $\psi(x_1,y_1)\phi(x_2,y_2).$ It does not yet have either required fermionic antisymmetry.

p.src:
First antisymmetrize the electron variables: $\Psi_x=
\psi(x_1,y_1)\phi(x_2,y_2)
-\psi(x_2,y_1)\phi(x_1,y_2).$ Under $x_1\leftrightarrow x_2$, the two terms exchange places and the whole expression changes sign. Now antisymmetrize this result in the proton variables. The four-term ordering is fixed by the two successive antisymmetrizations. $\begin{aligned}
\Psi_{2H}(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2)
&=\Psi_x(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}-\Psi_x(x_1,x_2;y_2,y_1)\\
&=\psi(x_1,y_1)\phi(x_2,y_2)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}-\psi(x_2,y_1)\phi(x_1,y_2)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}-\psi(x_1,y_2)\phi(x_2,y_1)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}+\psi(x_2,y_2)\phi(x_1,y_1).
\end{aligned}$ An electron exchange interchanges the first two terms and the last two terms, with an overall sign reversal. A proton exchange does the same. Thus the state has exactly the two separate antisymmetries required of the constituent fermions.

Indeed, exchanging the two atoms means making both substitutions $x_1\leftrightarrow x_2,
\qquad
y_1\leftrightarrow y_2.$ The first substitution contributes one fermionic minus sign and the second contributes another: $\begin{aligned}
\Psi_{2H}(x_2,x_1;y_2,y_1)
&=(-1)(-1)\Psi_{2H}(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2)\\
&=\Psi_{2H}(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2).
\end{aligned}$ The same result can be seen term by term in Eq. . Under the whole-atom exchange, $\psi(x_1,y_1)\phi(x_2,y_2)
\longleftrightarrow
\psi(x_2,y_2)\phi(x_1,y_1),$ so the first and fourth terms exchange. Likewise, $-\psi(x_2,y_1)\phi(x_1,y_2)
\longleftrightarrow
-\psi(x_1,y_2)\phi(x_2,y_1),$ so the second and third terms exchange. The complete state is symmetric under interchange of the atoms. Two constituent minus signs give the composite a plus sign.

The constituent exclusion is visible by testing coincidence directly. If the two modeled electron arguments coincide, $x_1=x_2=x$, Eq.  gives $\begin{aligned}
\Psi_{\mathrm{same}}(x,x;y_1,y_2)
&=2\bigl[
\psi(x,y_1)\psi(x,y_2)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}-\psi(x,y_1)\psi(x,y_2)
\bigr]\\
&=0.\end{aligned}$ The corresponding expression also vanishes when $y_1=y_2$. Thus the same-state composite wavefunction is nonzero, while its amplitude at coincident identical-fermion arguments vanishes.

p.src: The mathematics of spin recurs in isospin, color, and the other internal symmetries of particle physics. The analogy is formal: the same algebra appears, although the physical quantities need not have the same interpretation. The immediate task is to develop spin a little further and then return to the Dirac equation. This machinery will later be used for isospin, a concept associated historically with the 1930s.

An electron is a spin-$\tfrac12$ particle, as are the proton and the muon. Its $z$-component of spin has two possible values. Before setting units, write $S_z=m\hbar.$ From now on $\hbar=1$. The letter $L$ is conventionally reserved for orbital angular momentum, so intrinsic spin will be denoted by $S$. It obeys the same angular-momentum algebra: $=iS_z,
\quad
[S_y,S_z]=iS_x,
\quad
[S_z,S_x]=iS_y,$ and $S_\pm=S_x\pm iS_y.$ The operator $S_+$ raises the $S_z$ eigenvalue and $S_-$ lowers it.

p.src:
For spin one-half the only $S_z$ eigenvalues are $+\tfrac12$ and $-\tfrac12$. Suppress everything else about the electron for the moment: forget its position and momentum and retain only the two spin states. Then $|\psi\rangle
=
\alpha|\uparrow_z\rangle+\beta|\downarrow_z\rangle
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha\\
\beta
\end{pmatrix},$ where $|\alpha|^2=P(\uparrow_z),
\qquad
|\beta|^2=P(\downarrow_z),
\qquad
|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1.$ This is a two-dimensional state space. It is not a claim that ordinary space has two dimensions.

p.src:
Let $v=
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha\\
\beta\\
\gamma
\end{pmatrix}.$ Then $S_zv
=
\begin{pmatrix}
i\beta\\
-i\alpha\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.$ For eigenvalue $+1$, $i\beta=\alpha,
\qquad
-i\alpha=\beta,
\qquad
0=\gamma.$ Thus $\beta=-i\alpha$ and $\gamma=0$. Normalization gives $2|\alpha|^2=1$, so $|m=+1\rangle
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
-i\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.$ For eigenvalue $-1$, $i\beta=-\alpha,
\qquad
-i\alpha=-\beta,
\qquad
0=-\gamma,$ hence $\beta=i\alpha$, $\gamma=0$, and $|m=-1\rangle
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
i\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.$ Finally, the zero-eigenvalue equation gives $\alpha=\beta=0$, leaving $\gamma$ arbitrary. Its normalized solution is $|m=0\rangle
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.$ There are no further eigenvalues: these three eigenvectors exhaust the three-dimensional space. The factors $1/\sqrt2$ are not cosmetic. The same coefficients later enter quantitative experimental predictions when the algebra is applied to isospin.

p.src:
A moving spin-one-half particle is described by a position-dependent spinor, $\psi(x)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\psi_\uparrow(x)\\
\psi_\downarrow(x)
\end{pmatrix}.$ The quantities $\rho_{\uparrow_z}(x)=|\psi_\uparrow(x)|^2,
\qquad
\rho_{\downarrow_z}(x)=|\psi_\downarrow(x)|^2$ are joint position-and-spin probability densities. Their sum, $\rho(x)=\psi^\dagger(x)\psi(x)
=|\psi_\uparrow(x)|^2+|\psi_\downarrow(x)|^2,$ is the position density. If the particle is known to have been detected at $x$, then the conditional probabilities are $P(\uparrow_z\mid x)
=
\frac{|\psi_\uparrow(x)|^2}{\psi^\dagger(x)\psi(x)},
\qquad
P(\downarrow_z\mid x)
=
\frac{|\psi_\downarrow(x)|^2}{\psi^\dagger(x)\psi(x)},$ whenever $\rho(x)\neq0$. Thus an electron is represented by a two-component spatial wavefunction, with the local spin amplitudes allowed to vary from place to place.

p.src:
For example, $\begin{aligned}
|m=+1\rangle
&=
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
-i\\
0
\end{pmatrix}
\\
\Longrightarrow\quad\langle m=+1|
&=
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&i&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$ The projection amplitude is therefore $\begin{aligned}
\langle m=+1|\phi(x)\rangle
&=
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&i&0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi_1(x)\\
\phi_2(x)\\
\phi_3(x)
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=
\frac{\phi_1(x)+i\phi_2(x)}{\sqrt2}.\end{aligned}$ Applying the same rule to all three eigenvectors gives the spin-resolved densities. $\begin{aligned}
\rho_{+1}(x)
&=
\frac12\left|\phi_1(x)+i\phi_2(x)\right|^2,\\
\rho_{-1}(x)
&=
\frac12\left|\phi_1(x)-i\phi_2(x)\right|^2,\\
\rho_0(x)
&=
|\phi_3(x)|^2.\end{aligned}$ They satisfy $\begin{aligned}
\rho_{+1}(x)+\rho_{-1}(x)+\rho_0(x)
&=
|\phi_1(x)|^2+|\phi_2(x)|^2
\\
&\quad{}+|\phi_3(x)|^2
\\
&=
\phi^\dagger(x)\phi(x).
\end{aligned}$ If the particle is conditioned to have been detected at $x$, then $P(m\mid x)
=
\frac{\rho_m(x)}{\phi^\dagger(x)\phi(x)},$ provided $\phi^\dagger(x)\phi(x)\neq0$. The general measurement rule is always the same: form the bra of the desired normalized eigenvector, project the actual state onto it, and take the modulus squared. The resulting density retains its position dependence.

p.src:
The mixed terms must vanish. For different spatial directions, and also between every $\alpha_i$ and $\beta$, this gives $\alpha_i\alpha_j+\alpha_j\alpha_i=0

\alpha_i\beta+\beta\alpha_i=0.$ Equivalently, $\{\alpha_i,\alpha_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I_4,
\quad
\{\alpha_i,\beta\}=0,
\quad
\{\beta,\beta\}=2I_4.$ Each matrix anticommutes with every different matrix, while its anticommutator with itself is twice the identity.

p.src:
The four entries of $\Psi$ are not the four coordinates of spacetime. They are coordinates in the smallest vector space on which this anticommutation algebra can act. There are two distinct twofold structures: the division into $2\times2$ blocks and the two-component Pauli structure within each block. Anticipating the interpretation established below, the four possibilities may be organized as $\begin{array}{c|cc}
& S_z=+\tfrac12 & S_z=-\tfrac12\\ \hline
\omega>0 & (\omega>0,+\tfrac12) & (\omega>0,-\tfrac12)\\
\omega<0 & (\omega<0,+\tfrac12) & (\omega<0,-\tfrac12)
\end{array}.$ The lower row consists of negative-frequency electron states. It is not a row of positrons; a positron will be interpreted as a hole in the filled set of those states.

\psi_-

\psi_+
\end{pmatrix}.$ The rest-frame equation therefore becomes $i\frac{\partial\psi_+}{\partial t}=m\psi_-,
\qquad
i\frac{\partial\psi_-}{\partial t}=m\psi_+.$

p.src:
There are two natural suggestions. Taking another time derivative would decouple the system, but adding and subtracting the two equations diagonalizes them immediately. Indeed, $\begin{aligned}
i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\psi_++\psi_-)
&=m(\psi_++\psi_-),\\
i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\psi_+-\psi_-)
&=-m(\psi_+-\psi_-).\end{aligned}$ Defining $\chi_+=\psi_++\psi_-,
\qquad
\chi_-=\psi_+-\psi_-,$ gives two independent equations, $i\partial_t\chi_+=m\chi_+,
\qquad
i\partial_t\chi_-=-m\chi_-.$ For definite-frequency dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$, the sum has $\omega=+m,$ while the difference has $\omega=-m.$ This is exactly the positive- and negative-energy doubling found in the earlier one-dimensional example: the relativistic equation again has positive-energy and negative-energy electron solutions. Thus the block doubling separates into positive- and negative-energy branches. Pure rest-frame states may be written $\Psi_{\omega=+m}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\xi\\
\xi
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Psi_{\omega=-m}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\xi\\
-\xi
\end{pmatrix},$ where $\xi$ is still an arbitrary two-component object.

p.src: The negative-frequency branch leads to the Dirac-sea interpretation. A negative frequency is assigned negative electron energy. Filling every negative-energy electron state lowers the energy as far as the exclusion principle permits, since only one electron can occupy each complete fermionic state. The completely filled negative-energy sea is then called the vacuum.

p.src: Promote one electron from this filled sea into a positive-energy state. The result contains a positive-energy electron and an unoccupied negative-energy state. Removing a negative energy raises the energy, so the hole has positive excitation energy; because an electron is missing, it also carries the opposite electric charge. The hole is a positron.

p.src: The algebra has therefore produced two consequences at once: positive- and negative-energy branches, which become the particle–antiparticle structure, and a residual two-component structure associated with spin one-half. The striking point is that both emerged from the smallest matrices capable of satisfying the relativistic anticommutation relations. Spin had only recently appeared as an empirical property when this mathematical construction produced particles with spin together with an antiparticle branch; in that historical setting the result was dramatic.

p.src: A hole may participate in transitions. A positron has positive energy because it is the absence of a negative-energy electron. If a positive-energy electron fills the hole, the electron and positron annihilate, but their energy must be carried away, ordinarily by photons. In sea language, an electron has filled an unoccupied negative-energy state. The same release of energy can be pictured as an excited electron in an atom dropping to a lower level: the downward transition emits photons.

The original hole is filled, but the state from which that electron came is now empty. The hole has moved. Equivalently, the positron has changed its energy and has emitted radiation.
